==Education and early life==
Beddington was born on 23 March 1956, the second daughter of [[Roy Beddington|Roy]] and Anna Beddington (''née'' Griffith).<ref name=ttel01>{{cite news|title=Rosa Beddington|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/obituaries/1331245/Rosa-Beddington.html|access-date=20 October 2012|newspaper=The Telegraph|date=23 May 2001|location=London}}</ref>  She was raised with her elder sister, Pippa Beddington. She attended [[Sherborne School for Girls]] where she not only excelled in academics, but in her arts and sports programs as well. She later attended [[Brasenose College]], Oxford;<ref name=ttel01/> from 1974, obtaining a First in Physiological Sciences in 1977. She was the first woman to earn a first-class undergraduate degree at Brasenose.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Brazen Notes Issue 35 |url=https://www.bnc.ox.ac.uk/alumni/publications |access-date=2025-02-11 |website=www.bnc.ox.ac.uk}}</ref> Beddington embarked on the study of anterior-posterior axial patterning in mammalian embryos, beginning with her doctoral thesis entitled, "Studies on cell fate and cell potency in the postimplantation mammalian embryo"<ref>Beddington, Rosa. ''Studies on cell fate and cell potency in the postimplantation mammalian embryo''. 1981.</ref> supervised by Richard Gardner and Virginia Papaioannou,<ref name=FRS/> and was awarded a [[Doctor of Philosophy|DPhil]] in 1981.<ref name="phd">{{cite thesis |degree=PhD |first=Rosa |last=Beddington |title=Studies on cell fate and cell potency in the postimplantation mammalian embryo |publisher=University of Oxford |date=1981 |url=http://solo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/primo_library/libweb/action/dlDisplay.do?docId=oxfaleph016686176 |author-link=Rosa Beddington |archive-date=27 March 2022 |access-date=18 July 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220327135527/https://solo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/primo_library/libweb/action/dlDisplay.do?docId=oxfaleph016686176 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name=ttel01/>

==Career==
Beddington published numerous high-profile papers in her relatively short career (several important papers being published posthumously). She worked extensively on the developmental genetics of [[anterior|axial patterning]], [[germ layer]] specification, and other phenomena of [[gastrulation]] in mammals,<ref name=FRS /> including demonstrating that the [[primitive knot|node]] is the [[primitive knot|organizer]] in mammals.<ref>{{Cite journal
 | pmid = 8162859
| year = 1994
| last1 = Beddington
| first1 = R. S.
| title = Induction of a second neural axis by the mouse node
| journal = Development
| volume = 120
| issue = 3
| pages = 613–20
| doi = 10.1242/dev.120.3.613
}}</ref> Her technical contributions to experimental [[Embryogenesis|embryology]] include surgical re-implantation into the uterus to extend the time an experimentally manipulated embryo can be cultured<ref>{{Cite journal
 | pmid = 4078533
| year = 1985
| last1 = Beddington
| first1 = R. S.
| title = The development of 12th to 14th day foetuses following reimplantation of pre- and early-primitive-streak-stage mouse embryos
| journal = Journal of Embryology and Experimental Morphology
| volume = 88
| pages = 281–91
}}</ref> and the use of a [[transgenic]] marker ([[beta-galactosidase]]) to identify transplant versus host tissue in experimental embryos.<ref>{{Cite journal
 | pmid = 2483370
| year = 1989
| last1 = Beddington
| first1 = R. S.
| title = An in situ transgenic enzyme marker for the midgestation mouse embryo and the visualization of inner cell mass clones during early organogenesis
| journal = Development
| volume = 106
| issue = 1
| pages = 37–46
| last2 = Morgernstern
| first2 = J
| last3 = Land
| first3 = H
| last4 = Hogan
| first4 = A
| doi = 10.1242/dev.106.1.37
}}</ref>

While a fellow at the [[Cancer Research UK|Imperial Cancer Research Fund, (now Cancer Research UK)]] laboratory in Oxford, Beddington and [[Elizabeth Robertson (scientist)|Elizabeth Robertson]] recognised the potential of [[embryonic stem cell]]s for the study of genetic manipulation after demonstrating the ability of these cells to colonise developing embryos.<ref name="guardian"/><ref>{{Cite journal
 | pmid = 2598811
| year = 1989
| last1 = Beddington
| first1 = R. S.
| title = An assessment of the developmental potential of embryonic stem cells in the midgestation mouse embryo
| journal = Development
| volume = 105
| issue = 4
| pages = 733–7
| last2 = Robertson
| first2 = E. J.
| doi = 10.1242/dev.105.4.733
}}</ref>

Beddington taught at the newly established Cold Spring Harbor Laboratories summer course on manipulating the mouse embryo from 1986, including two years as co-organiser with Robertson.<ref name="FRS" /> Beddington was the meetings secretary for the British Society for Developmental Biology (BSDB) from 1990 to 1995. In 1993, she established and led a Division of Mammalian Development at the [[National Institute for Medical Research]].<ref name=ttel01/> She became on the first women to excel in this area of STEM at the time.

==Awards and honours==
[[File:Waddington medal.jpg|thumb|The Waddington medal designed by Rosa Beddington<ref name="FRS" />|left]]

A talented artist, she designed the Waddington Medal, awarded for outstanding performance and contribution to the field of [[developmental biology]]. Beddington herself received the Waddington Medal in 1999.<ref name="guardian"/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://bsdb.org/awards/the-waddington-medal/|access-date=12 October 2013|title=The Waddington Medal}}</ref> Additionally, the British Society for Developmental Biology has established in her honor The Beddington Medal, a national prize given for the most outstanding PhD dissertation in developmental biology in the previous year.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://bsdb.org/awards/the-beddington-medal/|access-date=12 October 2013|title=The Beddington Medal}}</ref> Its design is based upon drawings by Beddington. Her nomination for the Royal Society reads: {{centered pull quote|Beddington's work has combined classical [[embryology]] with [[molecular genetics]]. She has established using her great skills in [[Micromanipulator|micromanipulation]], many of the key features of gastrulation in the [[mouse]], a fundamental process in mammalian development. She was the first to demonstrate the axis-inducing activity of the mouse node and to show that the epiblast gives rise to all the adult organs. Most recently she has identified two [[homeobox]] [[gene]]s involved in the specification of anterior structures, including the forebrain. This work provides the first evidence that axial pattern in mammalian development originates in extra-embryonic tissue and that anterior identity is established before the formation of the primitive streak. It provides new insights into [[Regional specification|antero-posterior patterning]] throughout the [[vertebrate]]s.<ref name="royal"/>}}

==Personal life==
Beddington was married to [[Robin Denniston]].<ref name="whoswaswho"/> She died on 18 May 2001 from complications of cancer.<ref name=FRS>{{Cite journal | last1 = Rastan | first1 = Sohaila| last2 = Robertson | first2 = Elizabeth| author-link2 = Elizabeth Robertson| doi = 10.1098/rsbm.2005.0002 | title = Rosa Susan Penelope Beddington 23 March 1956 – 18 May 2001: Elected F.R.S. 1999 | journal = [[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]] | volume = 51 | pages = 15–32 | year = 2005 | doi-access = free }}</ref>
